title: Olbers' Paradox: Why Is the Night Sky Dark?
question: If the universe is infinite, eternal, and filled with stars, why isn't every point in the night sky as blazingly bright as the surface of the sun?
summary: A question simple enough for a child to ask turned out to require the Big Bang to answer properly. Olbers' Paradox—why the night sky is dark rather than uniformly ablaze with starlight—quietly encodes some of the deepest facts about the universe: that it had a beginning, that it is expanding, and that light itself takes time to arrive.
content:
Look up on a clear night and you see a scattering of bright points against overwhelming black. This seems too obvious to question—of course the sky is mostly dark, stars are far apart. But in a universe that is infinite, unchanging, and evenly sprinkled with stars, simple geometry predicts something starkly different: every single line of sight, in every direction, should eventually terminate on the surface of some star. The sky, far from being dark, should be a wall of light as bright as the sun. The night sky's darkness, treated as a genuine physics problem, is called Olbers' Paradox, and untangling it requires nothing less than the modern picture of a universe with a beginning.

The Geometry of the Problem

Consider shells of space at increasing distance from Earth, each shell twice as far away as the last. A shell at distance 2r has four times the surface area of a shell at distance r, so it contains roughly four times as many stars. But each of those stars, being twice as far away, appears only one-quarter as bright, by the inverse-square law of light. The extra number of stars and the reduced brightness per star cancel exactly—so each successive shell, no matter how distant, contributes the same total amount of light to the sky as the shell before it. Sum infinitely many equal, non-zero contributions and you get infinity. In a truly infinite, static, uniformly star-filled universe, the sky should be uniformly and unbearably bright, day or night, everywhere you look.

Why the Naive Fixes Don't Work

The first instinct is that distant stars are blocked by nearer ones, or that interstellar dust absorbs the light. Neither survives scrutiny: over infinite time, dust would simply absorb energy until it glowed as brightly as the stars heating it, re-radiating the light rather than hiding it. Blocking by intervening stars just means you'd eventually be staring at a star's surface instead of empty space, which is still bright, not dark. These explanations treat the symptom rather than the underlying assumption—and the underlying assumption that actually fails is the premise that the universe is infinite, static, and eternal in the simple sense Olbers, Kepler, and others originally imagined.

The Real Answer: A Universe With a Past

The paradox dissolves once you accept that the universe has a finite age—roughly 13.8 billion years since the Big Bang. Because light travels at a finite speed, we can only ever see stars whose light has had time to reach us; anything farther than about 13.8 billion light-years is, in principle, invisible to us not because it isn't there, but because its light hasn't arrived yet. The night sky is dark because the universe is young enough that most of the sky's potential light sources are still "in transit." Cosmic expansion compounds this: light from very distant, receding galaxies is redshifted out of the visible spectrum and diluted in energy, so even the light that does arrive from the deepest, oldest reaches of the observable universe is stretched into the faint microwave glow we call the cosmic microwave background—not blinding starlight, but a barely-there whisper only 2.7 degrees above absolute zero.

A Simple Observation, a Profound Consequence

What makes Olbers' Paradox remarkable is how much cosmology it smuggles in through the back door of a question anyone could ask while camping. The darkness of the night sky is direct observational evidence, available to the naked eye, that the universe is not infinite in age, or at least that it has not always looked as it does now—an argument for cosmic evolution that predates spectroscopy, redshift measurements, and the discovery of the cosmic microwave background by over a century. Heinrich Olbers formalized the puzzle in 1823; Edgar Allan Poe, of all people, sketched something close to the correct resolution in an 1848 prose poem, arguing that the finite speed of light and the universe's youth explained the darkness—beating professional astronomers to the answer by decades.

perspectives.title: Cosmology Perspective
perspectives.description: The dark night sky is direct empirical evidence that the universe has a finite age; because light travels at finite speed, we cannot yet see light from beyond roughly 13.8 billion light-years away, leaving most potential starlight still 'in transit.'

perspectives.title: Physics Perspective
perspectives.description: The inverse-square law and the growing surface area of distant shells cancel exactly in an infinite static universe, meaning the paradox is not resolved by dust, obstruction, or distance alone, but requires rejecting the static-infinite-eternal premise itself.

perspectives.title: History of Science Perspective
perspectives.description: The puzzle was named for Heinrich Olbers in 1823, but was anticipated by Kepler and others earlier, and partially solved with remarkable insight by Edgar Allan Poe in 1848, decades before the physics of cosmic expansion was understood.

perspectives.title: Observational Astronomy Perspective
perspectives.description: Cosmic expansion redshifts light from the most distant, oldest sources out of visibility entirely, diluting what would otherwise be additional starlight into the faint, uniform cosmic microwave background rather than a wall of visible light.

perspectives.title: Philosophy of Science Perspective
perspectives.description: Olbers' Paradox is a striking case where a mundane, universally available observation—the sky looks dark at night—served as genuine evidence against a specific cosmological model, long before technical instruments could test it directly.

connections: The Big Bang and the finite age of the universe

openQuestions: If the universe turns out to be infinite in spatial extent (even if finite in age), does that change how we should think about the total light 'waiting' to reach us in the far future?
How would the night sky look different to an observer billions of years from now, as more distant light continues to arrive?
Could there be other simple, everyday observations—like Olbers' darkness—that currently hint at deep facts about the universe we haven't yet recognized as evidence?
Does cosmic expansion accelerating due to dark energy mean some galaxies' light will never reach us at all, permanently capping how bright the night sky could ever become?
What does it say about scientific discovery that a poet, not a physicist, first sketched the correct resolution to a major cosmological puzzle?
